questions.q: Why does Mara build synthetic `datatable` scenarios in Sentinel's Logs blade before relying on this rule?
options: Because datatable is required syntax for every KQL query
Because a rule that compiles without error isn't the same claim as a rule that behaves correctly, and testing known scenarios is how you confirm the second one
Because Sentinel won't save a rule without a test table
Because real SigninLogs data can't be queried directly
questions.explain: The lesson's core point: "the query ran without an error" and "the query behaves correctly" are different claims, and only testing against known scenarios confirms the second.

questions.q: In Scenario 1 (six failures in five minutes, then a success at 09:06:00), what should the query return?
options: Zero rows, because six failures is too many
One result row, since this is the exact failures-then-success pattern the rule targets
Six result rows, one per failure
An error, because the time window is too short
questions.explain: This scenario is the true positive — a failure cluster immediately followed by a success is exactly what the rule was built to catch, so it should produce one matching row.

questions.q: In Scenario 2 (six failures, but no success ever follows), why does the query correctly return zero rows?
options: Because FailedCount never exceeds 5 in this scenario
Because the join kind=inner against Successes finds no matching successful sign-in to pair the failure cluster with
Because ResultType "50126" is not a valid failure code
Because the rule requires at least two different users
questions.explain: The Failures portion does flag this cluster, but the inner join has nothing on the Successes side to match against, so no row survives — correct behavior, not a bug.

questions.q: In Scenario 3 (one failure, then a success two minutes later), why does the query correctly stay silent?
options: Because the success happened too soon after the failure
Because a single failure never clears the FailedCount > 5 threshold, so the Failures query returns nothing for that user at all
Because ResultType "0" is treated as a failure
Because the join requires at least two users
questions.explain: This is the false-positive case the rule is specifically designed to avoid — an ordinary typo should never generate an incident, and FailedCount never reaches the threshold here.

questions.q: What would happen if this rule were deployed straight from Lesson 5 without the testing in this lesson?
options: Nothing different — testing is purely optional once the KQL syntax is correct
A subtle bug like a backwards join condition or an off-by-one time window could compile fine but still miss real attacks or flood the SOC with false alerts from ordinary typos
Sentinel would refuse to save the rule
The rule would automatically test itself on first run
questions.explain: A query can run without a syntax error and still be logically wrong — testing against known scenarios is what catches that before the rule is trusted with real traffic.
